You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 8 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

I'm starting on a robot arm, and the first joint is an MG996R servo. Could I 3D print a plate that holds the servo with its shaft sticking up? It should screw on through the servo's mounting tabs and sit firm, with no wobble. I'll work out how the plate fixes to the base later. I've got the servo here, and the screws, nuts and washers on your list.

Measurements I took:
- servo body length: 40.58 mm (the case, end to end, not counting the tabs)
- servo body width: 19.82 mm (the case, side to side)
- servo body height: 40.4 mm (the case, top to bottom)
- servo tab holes: 4.58 mm (each mounting tab has two holes, open to the tab's end like a U)
- servo hole spacing: 44.61 mm (between the holes on the two tabs, from the inside edge of one to the inside edge of the other; I didn't measure the spacing between the two holes on one tab)
- servo tab thickness: 2.28 mm
- servo tab to top: 5.63 to 5.69 mm (from the top face of a tab (the shaft side) to the top of the case)
- servo rib width: 1.51 mm (a rib on each tab's top face (the shaft side), between the tab's two holes; it stops the tabs sitting flush)
- servo rib height: 1.8 mm (how far the rib stands up from the tab's top face)
- servo rib position: 8.31 mm (from the side of the holes to the middle of the rib)
- servo cable exit: out of one end of the case, below the tabs (where the cable leaves; I didn't measure its size or how far it sticks out)

reasoning:
I'm sketching out a plate design with only eight turns to work with, so I need to pin down the key dimensions first. The MG996R servo body is about 40.5 by 19.8 mm, with mounting tabs that extend the overall length to roughly 54.5 mm. The holes run about 49.5 mm apart center to center along the length, and each tab carries two holes spaced around 10 mm across the width.

I'm checking the hole positions against the measured values: about 44.6 mm between inside edges works out to roughly 49.2 mm center to center, which fits the 49.5 mm spec. Still missing are the spacing between the two holes on one tab, the cable exit size, and the tab width, so I'll take those measurements next. I'm also settling how the plate sits: with the shaft up and the body hanging through a cutout, the tabs rest on the plate's top face, so the rib detail on the tab doesn't matter and the screws come down through the plate with nuts in pockets underneath.

I'm checking whether the screw head and washer can sit on the tab's top face between the two holes, since the rib there is narrow and the washer may hit it. Plugging in the numbers, the head clears the rib but a 9 mm washer would clash, so I'm leaning toward dropping the top washer and putting one under the plate instead. I still need the exact spacing from the side of the holes to the rib's center to confirm this.

I'm still weighing whether the rib sits too close to the holes to clear the screw head, and I need the exact distance from the holes to the rib's center to settle it. Next I'll measure the hole spacing across the tab, the tab width, and the cable exit, plus confirm M4 fits the 4.58 mm holes.

reasoning:
The person has given all the information they can, so I'll have to design around the unknowns and flag which numbers are guesses. The hole spacing across the tab hasn't been measured; I'm estimating roughly 10 mm from the MG996R datasheet. I'm also weighing whether a small test coupon with the hole pattern would be worth suggesting, or whether a design that doesn't depend on that spacing is the better route.

I'm weighing whether a slot across the tab width would let the screws be positioned without knowing the exact hole spacing, since the clamping would still hold. A fixed hole pattern would be tidier, though, so I'm also considering how the servo body's cutout in the plate could locate it independently of the tabs.

I'm working out whether the rib's position implies the hole spacing: if the 8.31 mm figure runs from the hole center to the rib, the spacing would be about 16.6 mm, but that leaves almost no edge margin on a 19.82 mm wide tab, so that reading looks doubtful.

I'm leaning toward slotted screw holes across the tab width, since the MG996R spacing is only a guess and the slots would let the clamps still hold if it's off by a couple of millimetres. I'm also checking whether the rib position implies a spacing near 12 mm, though a 10 mm recollection of the datasheet conflicts with that, so I'll flag the number as unresolved.

I'm settling on slotted screw holes across the tab width, since the hole spacing is still an estimate and the slots would let the clamps hold if it's off. The slot length would need to cover the range from about 9.5 to 12.6 mm centre to centre, with the nut pocket sized for M4.

I'm settling on the nut pocket: an elongated hex pocket with flats parallel to the slot so the nut can't spin, sized for M4 and about 3.2 mm deep. I also want to check whether the open U-shape at the tab end could let the tab slide out from under the screw head, since the slot is open there.

I'm checking whether the washer clears the rib at the tighter spacing, and it doesn't: a 9 mm washer would bump the rib at 9.5 mm centres. I'm dropping the top washer and keeping the head bearing directly on the tab, since the head is only 7 mm across and still covers the open end.

I'm checking the screw length: with the 2.28 mm tab and the 6 mm plate, an M4x10 reaches past the nut pocket at the bottom of the plate.

I'm choosing M4x10 over M4x8, since the 8 mm screw would only engage about 2.9 mm of the nut thread. The 10 mm screw sticks out roughly 1.7 mm below the plate, so I'll need to check that it clears the base.

I'm checking the tip length for an M4x8 screw against the 2.28 mm tab and a 6 mm plate, and it comes out at about zero, so there's no clean fit either way. I'm weighing whether to keep the M4x10 and note that the base needs about 1.7 mm of clearance below the plate.

Settling on an M4x10 screw here: the M4x8 would only engage about 2.9 mm of the nut thread and leaves the tip almost flush, so the longer screw gives more reliable engagement. The 1.7 mm that sticks out below the plate will need clearance from the base.

I'm settling on M4x8 with a 6 mm plate, which leaves the screw tip flush inside the nut pocket and the ceiling about 2.4 mm thick over the hole. Engagement is around 2.9 mm, which should be enough for a servo mount. The M4 clearance holes at 4.4 mm wide fit the slots, and the servo's 4.58 mm holes also take an M4 screw. I'm moving on to the cutout size for the body, 40.58 by 19.82 mm, with 0.4 mm clearance added.

I'm sizing the cutout for the servo body at about 41.2 by 20.4 mm, with a small clearance on each side. The open question is where the cable leaves the case, since it could sit inside the plate's thickness, so I'm considering a wide notch cut through the end of the plate to give it room.

I'm sizing the notch for the cable exit at the end of the plate, a bit under 8 mm wide so it clears a 3-pin connector, and cutting it through the full plate thickness out to the edge.

I'm checking where the cable can leave the plate, since the slots take up most of the width at the tab end and a notch of 8 mm would cut straight into them. I'm considering a channel on the underside of the plate instead, to see whether the cable can run out below the tabs without touching the screw pockets.

I'm checking where the cable leaves the case: on the MG996R it seems to come out of the lower part of one end, a bit below the tab line. If it sits more than about 6 mm under the tabs, it would clear the plate entirely.

I'm weighing a wider notch at the cable end of the cutout, but the slots sit close enough that a notch of that width would run into their inner edges.

I'm checking the nut pocket against the cutout edge: if the pocket is oriented with its flats along the length, it reaches about 7.9 mm past the body end and leaves almost no wall. I'm thinking about rotating it so the corners point along the length instead, which would change how much room the hex has.

I'm checking the nut pocket against the cutout wall: oriented with its flats along the length, it leaves only about 0.4 mm of plate between the pocket and the body opening, which is too thin. I'm weighing whether the pocket can be turned or the cutout narrowed locally instead.

I'm checking the nut pocket against the cutout wall, and the problem is that the plate between them is only about 0.4 mm thick along the whole slot region, which is too thin to hold. I'm thinking about either opening the pockets into the cutout or putting the cutout and pockets on separate sides.

I'm checking the nut pocket against the cutout edge: with the flats running along the length, the pocket's inner side sits only about 0.65 mm beyond the body end. Since the nut has to be at least 7 mm across the flats, that leaves almost no wall once clearance is included.

I'm weighing whether an M3 screw would give enough wall between the nut pocket and the cutout, since the M4 version leaves only about 0.35 mm.

I'm weighing an M3 screw against the M4, since the M3 nut leaves enough wall at the cutout end. A 7 mm washer would span the U-shaped slot and keep the head from pulling through, and it still clears the rib at either spacing. I'm also wondering whether the M4 nut could be made to work by reshaping the pocket outward instead.

I'm checking whether the nut pocket can work with the screw centered where it is, and the thin wall on its inner side is still the problem. I'm considering whether the M3 option or a different pocket orientation handles that better.

I'm weighing a tight-fit option for the cutout, but that feels risky with printing tolerances, so I'm considering a different clamping idea instead: holding the tabs from above with the plate rather than from below with a nut. The ribs would then keep the tabs from sitting flush, and the shaft has only about 5.6 mm of height above the tab to work with.

I'm considering a different layout where the plate sits on top of the tabs instead, so the nut pocket goes in the top face and the body top fits into a cutout. That would also mean the ribs need relief grooves on the plate's underside.

I'm weighing whether the nut pocket can sit on the underside without breaking into the cutout, since the pocket depth and the ceiling thickness would have to share the same vertical space. A thinner plate or a shallower pocket might work, but it gets tight quickly. Another route is to keep M4 and make the cutout only as large as needed to locate the body, rather than a full rectangle.

I'm settling on an M3 screw for the clamp, since its nut pocket leaves a workable wall of about 1.1 mm against the cutout. The washer should be around 7 mm across so it spans the U-shaped slot. I'll keep the M4 option in mind only if that wall proves too thin in practice.

I'm settling the screw slots: with the M3 option the slot can be about 3.4 mm long and centred on the tab hole, which sits roughly 4.3 mm past the body end. That leaves room for ±0.6 mm of offset, so the cutout still does the locating while the screws just clamp.

Working out the slot spacing now: the hole centres work out to about 49.2 mm apart, which puts the screw roughly 4.3 mm past the body end. Across the width I'm still only guessing between 10 and 12 mm centres, so the slot should allow for a screw centre swinging around 4.8 to 6.2 mm from the midline.

I'm settling the nut pocket's shape now: a hexagon with its flats set so the pocket's length runs across the width, which needs roughly 6.6 mm of span once the clearance is added.

I'm working out the hexagonal nut pocket's orientation now: with the vertices set along the length axis, the flats face across the width, and the hexagon is stretched into a slot by hulling two copies at different positions.

Working out the nut pocket geometry now: a hexagon centred at each end of the slot, with a rectangle joining them, and the inner wall between opposing pockets still leaves about 3 mm of clearance.

I'm checking the plate dimensions against the pocket positions: the pockets reach about 9.6 mm out from the centreline while the cutout only extends to 10.2 mm, so they clear each other along the length. That puts the overall plate near 68 mm by 36 mm, with the nut pockets sitting beyond the body ends.

I'm checking the cutout against the pocket positions: the inner pocket edge clears the cutout end by about 1.1 mm. Next I'm considering where the cable leaves the case, since a notch in the plate would have to fit in the narrow gap between the pockets.

I'm wondering whether the cable exit sits far enough below the tab to clear a 6 mm plate, since I don't know that height. If it doesn't, a short test coupon with one slotted end and the cutout wall could confirm the fit before printing the full part.

I'm considering a small coupon as a test piece: just the end of the plate with the cutout open on the inner side, so I can check the tab and screw fit before printing the full part. For the cable, I'm thinking about adding a narrow relief notch in the cutout end wall so the wiring has room to leave.

I'm weighing whether the cable exit clears a 6 mm plate, since I don't know how far below the tab it sits. I'll flag that as an unknown to check before printing, and I'm not going to add a cable relief that would only fit in the narrow gap between the pockets.

I'm working out the screw length now: the washer, the 2.28 mm tab, the roughly 3.2 mm of plate left above the nut pocket, and the nut itself add up to about 8 mm, so an M3x8 screw should do it.

I'm checking the screw length against the actual stack: head washer, the 2.28 mm tab, and the 6 mm plate, which puts the tip around 1 mm below the plate bottom. An M3x10 would overshoot, so M3x8 looks like the better fit, leaving the tip just short of the bottom face with the nut seated at the ceiling.

Checking the screw length against the nut pocket: an M3x8 leaves the tip about 0.8 mm above the plate bottom, which still engages roughly 2 mm of the nut thread. Nut insertion from the underside is next.

I'm checking that the washer and rib don't interfere with the plate, and they don't, since the washer rests on the tab and the rib sits on top. Next I'm looking at how the servo body hangs through the full 6 mm cutout.

I'm setting the plate's outer size next: the nut pockets reach about 27.5 mm from centre, so with a 6 mm margin the plate runs roughly 67 mm long and 36 mm wide. I'm also keeping the parameter list to the measured body and tab dimensions plus the screw and nut sizes, with no extra features added yet.

I'm turning to the joints now: four screw joints on the plate, each with its origin at the washer seat, roughly 8.78 mm up from the plate face, pointing downward through the slot and the nut pocket.

Now I'm settling the plate's parameters and writing the build function, describing the plate's dimensions and the slot centres in code form.
